reading.title: The Shortcut Above Maple Creek
reading.purpose: Follow a hillside town learning how quick fixes can trigger unexpected consequences.
paras: When summer traffic jammed the narrow bridge into Pineview, the town board voted to pave a steep shortcut through the woods above Maple Creek. Supporters promised faster commutes by October. Nobody paused to study every ramification—every complicated, unexpected consequence that might ripple outward once bulldozers stripped away a hundred mature oaks.

The first warning arrived in November. Without tree roots gripping the slope, heavy rain washed red clay down into the creek, turning the water murky. That quick fix began to backfire, producing the exact opposite of the smooth travel residents wanted when mudslides closed the new road twice in one week. To patch the washouts, crews dumped loose gravel along the shoulder, which only served to compound the problem by adding even more runoff to the ditches below.

Soon the wider town felt each unwelcome repercussion. Clogged culverts flooded three basements near the mill, and every passing truck seemed to exacerbate the ruts, making the damaged hillside worse after each storm. "It was almost inevitable," retired surveyor Mr. Cho told the council, "because water always finds the steepest path once you remove the trees." Worse still, the landslide carved away an old spring-fed fern glade, an irreversible loss that no repair crew could ever restore.

At the December meeting, eighth grader Nadia showed aerial photos proving the cumulative damage—how small weekly washouts had piled up into a major gully over three months. She warned that paving another hillside trail would set a dangerous precedent, an example that developers would cite again and again to justify risky shortcuts and perpetuate the same cycle of erosion. By spring, the town closed the shortcut, planted three hundred saplings, and wrote a new rule requiring slope studies before any road was approved.

qs.q: In paragraph 4, the word "cumulative" most nearly means
choices: happening only once during a single autumn rainstorm
growing larger as small effects pile up over time
easy to undo by planting saplings beside a creek
approved quickly without a full town board vote
qs.why: Paragraph 4 defines cumulative directly as "how small weekly washouts had piled up into a major gully over three months."

qs.q: Which sentence shows how the crews' repair attempt actually made the runoff worse?
choices: The first warning arrived in November.
Without tree roots gripping the slope, heavy rain washed red clay down into the creek, turning the water murky.
That quick fix began to backfire, producing the exact opposite of the smooth travel residents wanted when mudslides closed the new road twice in one week.
To patch the washouts, crews dumped loose gravel along the shoulder, which only served to compound the problem by adding even more runoff to the ditches below.
qs.why: This sentence explains that dumping loose gravel added even more runoff to the ditches below, compounding the washout problem.

ev.text: To patch the washouts, crews dumped loose gravel along the shoulder, which only served to compound the problem by adding even more runoff to the ditches below.

qs.q: Why did Nadia warn the council about setting a precedent with the paved shortcut?
choices: Developers could point to it later to justify more risky roads that repeat the same erosion.
The town board wanted to build three new bridges across Maple Creek by October.
Aerial photographs are too expensive for most eighth graders to take in winter.
Planting saplings takes longer than pouring loose gravel along a steep shoulder.
qs.why: Paragraph 4 explains that paving another trail would give developers an example to cite again and again, perpetuating erosion.

qs.q: What is the main lesson of this story?
choices: Narrow bridges should never be repaired once summer traffic begins to slow down.
Rushing a quick fix without weighing long-term consequences can create bigger, lasting problems.
Loose gravel is the best material for stopping mudslides on steep forested hills.
Retired surveyors should make all road decisions without holding public town meetings.
qs.why: The town's shortcut backfires into mudslides, flooded basements, and irreversible habitat loss, teaching them to require slope studies first.
